en: Was fitted snugly at his wrist.
Beyond him came
Kanchoro, son of Chubak—
Huge as half a mountain,
Fit to overcome any opponent,
His courage precious, his wrath strong,
He leveled whoever attacked.
This was the strength bound at the waist,
This was the hero left as a legacy!
The figure there in front
Was the young son of Manas,
His support on the road to Beijing!
His form was like a craggy mountain,
From lion hero Chubak,
The young man left as a support.
Semetey's dependable men,
Kanchoro and Külchoro,
The two dependable twins,
His sole companions at the cairn,
The comrades who would support
Your mighty Semetey.
When their figures came forward,
Yesterday, preparing to besiege Kakan,
As your dear prince stood there,
Like an army of six divisions appeared
The figures of those two.
Külchoro rode
Hero Toltoi's Surkoön.
Kanchoro rode
Khan Köbösh's Köktelki.
It never tired when ridden on reconnaissance,
Never ailed when ridden with the baggage train,
Never wearied when ridden into gunfire;
Until it reached sixty years,
Its tusklike teeth did not age.
Unless not a handspan of rein remained,
It would not yield to a determined foe;
Unless a thousand true disasters struck,
It would not let its rider be felled.
Driving fourteen horses from Ogoy,
Saying, “I shall gird my waist firmly,
From Kongurbai in Beijing
I shall exact my heroic father's blood-price.
Kongurbai is the one I shall face;
I shall bring chaos.
If gracious God supports me,
I shall avenge the bloodthirsty hero.”
Settling himself like a lion,
For seething Beijing
The four warriors made ready.
Saying, “If death comes, I shall die;
The countless dark livestock gathered as tribute,
Kongurbai's myriad herds,
If I live, I shall raid and return.
Across the tops of the teeming herds
I shall ride,
The Kalmak who descended upon you—
I shall scatter all four kinds of his livestock.”
Angrily making ready,
With Khan Bakai at their head,
The bloodthirsty youth mounted.
His grandmother Chyiyrdy
And his own mother Kanykei
Had a white-gray mare caught,
Had it sacrificed to the moon-shaped hoof,
And spread their hands, saying, “Amen!”
The sorrowing elders
Spread not a few but many hands in prayer,
To the Forty Saints and Khizr-Ilyas,
Entrusting him to their protection,
To Manas, who had passed into eternity,
Dedicating him to his spirit,
They spread their hands, saying, “Amen!
The piebald-headed one is the tulpar among horses;
My orphan is setting out on a journey—
Reach him, heroes, and give him aid,
Almambet and Chubak among you!
May God set the undertaking right;
My heroes who passed away long ago,
Give aid to my only one!
If you turn toward Kakan and Beijing,
It will be a disgrace if you let him be taken;
To Almighty God
I entrust for safekeeping
The only one I gained through suffering!
Go safely and return unharmed,
My only one, whom I bore near death;
Come back quickly, without making us pine!
For six months we shall burn with longing;
Children, if you do not return in six months,
Give up hope of your mother—
We shall behold the face of the next world!
Parted from you, our only one,
What desire can we attain?
For the true place from which none return,
If you are delayed, we shall depart!
You will fight the Kakanchin;
May gracious Allah grant you a road,
And may your bloodthirsty falcon of a father
Come out upon your road and give you his hand!
You will fight Kongurbai;
May that infidel be brought low.
My foal, may what you accomplish
Remain, for the people of the final age,
A deed never to be forgotten!”
His two mothers gave their blessing,
Their hearts painfully torn,
And both mothers wept,
Tears pouring from their eyes.
When they wept in grief,
The people wept, wept blood;
Unable to cease their sorrow,
All the multitude wept,
As though they were about to part forever,
Their hearts painfully torn,
Their ribs seeming to split,
Tears pouring from their eyes.
Among the Argyn and Kyrgyz,
The khoja in a white turban wept,
The mullah with the white Quran wept;
All those people wept.
They sacrificed a mare to the moon-shaped hoof,
And, invoking Allah, sacrificed a camel;
For the young son of the prince,
All the Kyrgyz sobbed
And loudly gave their prayer.
In high spirits he drove fourteen horses,
Loading provisions upon the tulpar.
While the people grieved,
He received their blessing;
The Kakanchin was the foe he would fight;
The lion prince rode out.
From Kanykei's palace
His countless host set out on the journey;
The young son of the hero
Was bound for Beijing.
In high spirits he took fourteen horses,
Received the blessing of the saint,
And with Khan Bakai as their leader,
Your sovereign rode out.
Eagerly girding himself,
Straining and swaying,
Saying, “My journey is far;
Kongurbai is the one I shall fight,
And I shall avenge my father,”
The gray wolf traveled on in high spirits,
Taking the road toward the Kakanchin.
From the iron-gated fortress,
Just as the hero was leaving
Kanykei's palace,
He wore upon him
A double coat of ring mail.
At the mouth of the gate,
Your gray wolf happened to meet
Ayçürök, Akun's daughter.
The unfortunate daughter of Akun
Had many a sorrow!
With the beauty of an owl's plumage,
With a voice like a nightingale's,
Breathing musk and fragrant copper,
She spoke smoothly and asked,
Showing a white throat like an argali's,
Noble lady Ayçürök,
Her white breast rising.
The unfortunate daughter of the peri
Had a grace unlike mortal women;
The forlorn woman's words
Were sweeter than honey.
She walked with a soft, graceful stride,
Her eyes shining like the morning star.
Her white throat gleamed,
Her moonlike face shone.
Her gold earrings, large as bowls,
Sparkled upon her breast;
When she turned, she gave off perfume.
The renowned lady Ayçürök,
Turning like a peri-born beauty,
Walked in sorrowful grace,
Wrapped in a fine elechek.
Arching like a lynx,
Reluctant to utter her words,
She held herself like a white doe
And began to speak of every concern:
“My prince, you have set out on a six-month journey!
Let us come out to meet you on your return;
You have set forth to the people of the dark day—
Turn and speak to us before you go,
So that we too, though women, may hear!
You will fight the Kakanchin;
You have begun the journey to Beijing.
You have left your peerless wife,
The infidel woman of surpassing wisdom,
And sixty sisters-in-law widowed,
Leaving your camp desolate!
You set out without telling your secret;
My valiant one, we are hurt by you!
They say Beijing is a distant land;
What living soul inhabits Beijing?
Radiant Beijing—
No enemy who faced it ever prevailed.
From what I hear of the Kakanchin,
They are a people from whom none return!
Even your khan father did not go against
Those seething infidels.
No one who challenged
Kakanchin's Beijing remained alive.
They say the road to calamitous Beijing
Is one from which none return;
Even sultans entered but could not conquer
The grim-visaged Chinese!
Turn Buurul's head around;
Do not struggle, my prince—stay!
They say assembled Beijing
Has never been overcome by mortal man.
The heroes could not wreak slaughter,
From Beijing, though it had fallen into ruin,
The mighty could wrest no victory!
There is a teeming Chinese people;
When we ask the elders,
Everyone who challenges them—
They say it is their custom to drink their blood!
Going to confront Beijing,
Many renowned khans have died;
When we ask those who know,
They say all the heroes died!
Beijing is no easy land,
And the Chinese are no people upon whom to take revenge.
They are established as the Kakanchin,
A wing of grievous calamity;
It is their custom to drink the blood
Of everyone who challenges them!
Their chief, Tungsha, lies there;
Great Beijing and its many peoples—
Such is their tumult!
They answer only to themselves,
They say, those imperious Chinese;
Though ears have heard and eyes have seen,
No mortal man has conquered Beijing.
The people of Beijing are forty tribes,
Scattered in forty directions;
Of worldly abundance,
To stand as its pillar,
Almighty Allah the Creator made them!
To make war
Upon radiant Beijing—
I, a wretched and fierce-tempered woman,
Have had my good fortune consumed!
To say you will conquer
Machyn, Kakan, and Bakburchun,
To say you will make war
On the eminent, ancient Chinese people—
That is you consuming my good fortune!
Understand every word I say!
Do not scorn me as a woman;
Lion prince, heed my words!
